summary: The compile_kernel / _kernel_partition / params-jitability suites are exceptionally thorough: discovery/demotion, fusion-minimality (brute-force optimality check), diamond/fan-out/reconvergent boundary, recompute cones (LRU cache, eviction, type-change flush-and-reseed, interior override, cross-process cache), declared eager Case A/B/C, return-type validation across plain/dispatcher/cres/cfunc/dufunc, and fingerprint collision/uncacheability are all covered. The genuine gaps are doc/API drift, not code-path coverage: the variable docs show a nonexistent `.variables` attribute on the `Variables` namespace, and two declared-kernel recompute paths (interior-override on a declared kernel; the `_evaluate`-seeded declared array/contract interplay) have no direct test. None are silent-wrong-result hazards.

findings.title: variable docs reference a nonexistent `.variables` attribute on the Variables namespace
findings.claim: The docs registry example accesses `variables1.variables.keys()` / `variables2.variables.keys()` and `variables1.variables["x"]`. The `Variables`/`Namespace` class has no public `variables` attribute -- the dict is stored as the private `_variables` and exposed via `keys()` / `__getitem__`. A user copy-pasting this snippet gets an `AttributeError`. The matching test (test_variable.py:54,57) uses the correct `variables1.keys()` / `variables1["x"]`, so the docs have drifted from the real API.
findings.evidence: variable.py line 14 `_variables: dict[str, 'Variable']`, line 216 `self._variables = {variable["name"]: ...}`, line 17 `def keys(self): return self._variables.keys()`, line 218 `def __getitem__(self, variable_name: str)`. A grep for a public `.variables` member returns nothing (only `_variables`). The docs block (rst literal block opened by the trailing `::` on line 118) reads `assert list(variables1.variables.keys()) == ["x", "a"]` and `assert isinstance(variables1.variables["x"], Variable)`. test/core/test_variable.py:54 asserts `list(variables1.keys()) == ["x", "a"]` and line 57 `isinstance(variables1["x"], Variable)` -- the correct surface.
findings.recommendation: Change the doc snippet to `variables1.keys()` / `variables1["x"]` (matching test_variable.py and the `Namespace.keys`/`__getitem__` API). Note this block is an rst `::` literal block, which doc-codeblock-flake8 does NOT extract (extract_codeblocks.py only matches `.. code-block:: python` / `.. code:: python`), so CI will not catch it -- fix manually.

findings.title: No test for recompute interior-override on a declared (eager) kernel
findings.claim: `CompiledKernel._apply_changes` has a declared-kernel branch that runs the `can_convert` contract check on interior overrides too (an interior name resolving via ordered_nodes), and `_expand_sources` rebuilds the boundary / clears the cone cache. The undeclared interior-override path is well tested (test_compile_kernel.py test_recompute_interior_override_matches_interpreted / _expands_sources_and_flushes / _yield_distinct_keys), but no test overrides an INTERIOR node on a declared (is_declared True) kernel. The declared branches `self.is_declared and _is_typed(var)` in _apply_changes are only exercised for EXTERNAL changes (test_declared_recompute_off_contract_type_raises_crisp, test_case_a/b_recompute). A regression that mis-resolved an interior override under the declared contract (e.g. wrongly type-checking against a declared interior type, or skipping source expansion) would pass CI.
findings.evidence: compile_kernel.py lines 534-549: `var = next((n.variable for n in compiled.ordered_nodes if n.variable.qual_name() == qual), None)` then `if self.is_declared and _is_typed(var): ... can_convert(...)`. The declared interior-override case is reachable but untested: declared recompute tests in test_params_jitability.py (lines 172-175, 253-258, 305-315, 318-331, 366-369) all change `{"e": {"x": ...}}` (an external), never an interior node such as `{"c": {"a": ...}}`.
findings.recommendation: Add a declared-kernel recompute test that overrides an interior node (e.g. `ck.recompute({"c": {"a": <val>}})` on `_graph_all_jittable`), asserting the value matches the interpreted oracle and that an off-contract interior value raises the crisp `declared type` error.

findings.title: _evaluate seeding for a declared kernel with a demoted (Case B) node is not directly exercised by recompute
findings.claim: `_ensure_store` for a declared kernel calls `_evaluate(..., self._demoted)` instead of `discover`, seeding interior values from the frozen declared demotion set. test_case_b_recompute (test_params_jitability.py 253-258) does drive a Case-B (declared, demoted middle node) recompute, so the demoted branch of `_evaluate` (line 336 `elif var in demoted`) IS hit. But test_evaluate_honors_fixed_demotion_set (148-162) calls `_evaluate` directly with a Dispatcher-only binding set and never exercises the exotic-binding branch (line 333 `if not isinstance(binding, Dispatcher): ... _call_exotic`) under a declared recompute. A declared graph that mixes a cres/cfunc/dufunc node with a demoted node, then recomputes, would route through `_evaluate`'s exotic branch on the seeding pass -- a path with no test.
findings.evidence: _kernel_partition.py _evaluate lines 327-340: three branches -- exotic (`not isinstance(binding, Dispatcher)` -> `_call_exotic`), demoted-py (`elif var in demoted`), else Dispatcher. test_evaluate_honors_fixed_demotion_set builds `bindings = {a: _njit_t3(a.formula), b: _njit_t3(b.formula)}` (both Dispatchers), so the exotic branch is never taken; test_declared_exotic_node_end_to_end (426-438) builds a fused (Case A, no demotion) cres kernel and calls `kernel`, not `recompute`, so `_evaluate` is never invoked with both an exotic binding AND a demoted node.
findings.recommendation: Add a declared-mix test combining a cres/cfunc node and a declared `jitable=False` node, seed via a full call, then `recompute` an external -- asserting the result matches the interpreted oracle. This exercises `_evaluate`'s exotic branch on the declared seeding path.
